description: Putney Debates, Diggers on St George's Hill — the army's radical politics after victory.
content_html:
Why Did Radical Groups Emerge After 1645?

Military victory created new political problems. By 1646 Parliament had defeated the King, but the army that had won the war now demanded a say in the peace. The New Model Army was an unusual institution: its soldiers and junior officers debated theology, read pamphlets and believed God had given them victory for a purpose. This religious ferment, combined with practical grievances over pay and potential disbandment, made the army a political as well as military force.

The most significant radical group to emerge was the Levellers. The name — applied by their opponents, not themselves — implied they wanted to level social distinctions, which they denied. Their core demands were more limited but genuinely radical for the time: a widened franchise, equality before the law, religious toleration, and an end to imprisonment for debt.

Key Fact

The Levellers demanded: a widened male franchise (though not universal), equality before the law, freedom of conscience in religion, and an end to arbitrary imprisonment. They gathered most support among the rank and file of the New Model Army.

Key Figures: Lilburne and Rainsborough

John Lilburne was the Levellers’ most prolific pamphleteer. Imprisoned multiple times by both the King and Parliament, he argued that every freeborn Englishman had natural rights that no government could take away. Thomas Rainsborough gave the Levellers’ most memorable statement of principle at the Putney Debates: “The poorest he that is in England hath a life to live as the greatest he.” This is a documented quotation from the Clarke Papers, the written record of the debates. Rainsborough argued every man deserved a vote because every man was subject to the government.

The Putney Debates 1647

In October and November 1647, representatives of the army’s rank and file (called “agitators”) met senior officers including Cromwell and his son-in-law Henry Ireton in the Putney Debates. The Levellers presented their Agreement of the People, a draft written constitution. The central dispute was over the franchise: should all men vote, or only property owners?

Ireton argued that the vote should be restricted to those with “a permanent fixed interest in this kingdom” — that is, property owners. He feared that if all men voted, they would use their majority to abolish property rights. Rainsborough and the Levellers countered that a man without property still had an interest in his government because he was subject to its laws. The debate ended without resolution. Cromwell then used his authority to suppress the Leveller mutinies that followed, executing the ringleaders at Burford in 1649.

Even more radical than the Levellers were the Diggers. In April 1649 a small group led by Gerrard Winstanley began digging and planting on St George’s Hill in Surrey, claiming that the earth was a “common treasury” belonging to all people, not private landowners. The Diggers were never a mass movement — at their peak perhaps a few dozen people — but they represented the most thoroughgoing social radicalism of the period. Local landowners and the Council of State suppressed their communities within a year.

The Quakers and Religious Radicalism

Religious radicalism also flourished in the 1640s and 1650s. The Quakers, founded by George Fox around 1650, rejected all outward forms of worship, professional clergy and set prayers. They spoke of an “Inner Light” within every person. Quakers refused to doff their hats to social superiors and addressed everyone — including judges and magistrates — with the familiar “thee” and “thou” rather than formal titles. This made them extremely provocative to established authority. Other groups included the Ranters (who denied sin and conventional morality), the Fifth Monarchists (who believed Christ’s Second Coming was imminent), and the Muggletonians.

Key Fact

Thomas Rainsborough argued at the Putney Debates: “The poorest he that is in England hath a life to live as the greatest he.” This quotation is recorded in the Clarke Papers, the army secretary’s written record of the 1647 debates.

Parliament and the army leadership were deeply ambivalent about the radical groups. Religious toleration appealed to many Independents (who opposed a compulsory state church) but went too far for Presbyterians who wanted a new enforced orthodoxy. Political radicalism threatened property and social order in ways that alarmed both Parliament and army grandees. Cromwell suppressed the Leveller mutinies militarily. The Blasphemy Act of 1650 targeted the Ranters. The Diggers were dispersed by landlord pressure. The Quakers were imprisoned in large numbers under the Protectorate. Radical groups achieved very little immediate change but their ideas — especially the Leveller demand for wider suffrage — remained influential in later centuries.
exam_tip_html: Questions about radical groups often ask about their significance or the reaction of Parliament and the army. Don’t treat all radical groups as the same — Levellers sought political reform within a recognisable system; Diggers challenged property ownership itself; Quakers challenged religious and social hierarchy. Distinguish between them and explain why each threatened different sections of the establishment. The Rainsborough quotation (“The poorest he...”) is well-evidenced and worth using accurately in essays.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Levellers, led by Lilburne and supported by Rainsborough, demanded wider franchise, legal equality and religious toleration; the Putney Debates (1647) debated these demands directly within the army.
  • The Diggers (Gerrard Winstanley) challenged property ownership itself by communally cultivating common land at St George’s Hill from April 1649.
  • Parliament and army leadership suppressed radical groups — Cromwell crushed Leveller mutinies in 1649, and the Diggers were dispersed by landlord pressure within a year.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Leveller movement in the 1640s.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: The Levellers demanded a wider male franchise through their Agreement of the People, arguing that all men subject to government should have a say in choosing it, not just property owners.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Putney Debates of October to November 1647.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Army agitators presented the Agreement of the People, a draft written constitution demanding a widened franchise. Feature 2: Cromwell and Ireton opposed the franchise extension, arguing property ownership was necessary for political rights; the debates ended without agreement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Levellers gained support within the New Model Army in 1647.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more reasons explained with evidence (religious culture of the army, pay grievances, Lilburne's pamphlets, political vacuum after First Civil War, rank and file felt excluded from post-war settlement). Linked argument. Secure: Two causes. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Levellers were the most significant radical group of the 1640s. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument comparing Levellers (scale, programme, army influence, Putney Debates) with Diggers (more radical challenge to property) and Quakers (religious radicalism, longer survival). Reaches a supported judgement about relative significance. Secure: Compares two or more groups with evidence. Developing: Mainly discusses Levellers with limited comparison. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why radical religious and political groups emerged in England in the late 1640s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (breakdown of censorship, army as vehicle for radical ideas, religious pluralism encouraged by civil war, social dislocation, Calvinist emphasis on individual faith). Linked and developed. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament and the army suppressed the Levellers after the Putney Debates.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains why Leveller demands threatened property, social order and army discipline; Ireton's ideological opposition; Cromwell's priority for stability; Leveller mutinies gave military justification. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Agreement of the People?
flashcard_questions.a: Leveller draft written constitution demanding wider franchise and legal equality

flashcard_questions.q: What did Thomas Rainsborough argue at Putney?
flashcard_questions.a: Every man subject to the law deserves a vote — 'the poorest he hath a life to live'

flashcard_questions.q: Who led the Leveller movement as its main pamphleteer?

flashcard_questions.a: Senior army officer, Cromwell's son-in-law, who opposed the Leveller franchise demands

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Diggers do in April 1649?
flashcard_questions.a: Began communal cultivation on St George's Hill, Surrey, claiming land as common property

flashcard_questions.q: How did Cromwell respond to Leveller mutinies in 1649?
flashcard_questions.a: Suppressed them militarily, executing ringleaders at Burford

flashcard_questions.q: Why were Quakers provocative to authority?
flashcard_questions.a: Refused to remove hats for superiors; used 'thee/thou' for everyone, rejecting deference

glossary_terms.definition: A political movement of the 1640s demanding wider male suffrage, religious toleration, legal reform and a written constitution; they drew up the Agreement of the People.
Leading Leveller pamphleteer, repeatedly imprisoned for his writings; known as 'Freeborn John' for his defence of common legal rights.
Army officer and Leveller sympathiser whose speech at the Putney Debates articulated the case for wider franchise.
Senior army officer and Cromwell's son-in-law, who opposed the Levellers' franchise demands at the Putney Debates.
Series of debates held in the church of St Mary the Virgin, Putney, October–November 1647, between army grandees and Leveller agitators over the future constitution of England.
A group led by Gerrard Winstanley who began communal cultivation of common land at St George's Hill, Surrey in April 1649, arguing that the earth was a 'common treasury' for all.
A religious movement founded by George Fox around 1650, emphasising direct individual experience of God (the 'Inner Light') and rejecting formal clergy, churches and sacraments.

hero_image_caption: Radical groups debated the future of England in the aftermath of civil war.
